steps.title: Scope the UART core as a vendor-IP replacement behind a separate register wrapper
steps.goal: Write the Overview: a single-clock UART core (TX + RX + two FIFOs) for a GPS module and debug console. It is configured at runtime by divider and parity inputs, and it exposes valid/ready streams to a register wrapper owned by another team. State what is out of scope (registers, interrupts, flow control).

spec_evidence.quote: we need our own UART block instead of the vendor IP
It talks to a
the register wrapper is done
separately by another team.

options: Core exposes raw config inputs (divider, parity) and stream ports; wrapper owns registers and interrupts
Core includes its own CSR block
decisions.choice: The core exposes raw config input ports and valid/ready streams. Registers and interrupt logic live in the wrapper.
decisions.rationale: The spec says the register wrapper is done separately and the CPU side is a valid/ready stream.

done_when: Overview names the use cases (GPS, debug console), the target baud rates 9600 and 115200, and clocks of 50 MHz and 100 MHz.
Overview explicitly lists what is out of scope: CSRs, interrupt generation, RTS/CTS flow control, and configurable data or stop bit counts.

steps.title: Define the port list: serial pins, runtime config, TX/RX streams with per-byte error sideband, and overflow/status
steps.goal: Enumerate every port with direction, width, and meaning. This covers clk, reset, rxd, txd, the divider input, parity enable/odd inputs, the TX input stream, and the RX output stream carrying data plus frame/parity error flags. It also covers the overflow indication and FIFO status outputs useful to the wrapper.

spec_evidence.quote: The CPU side should look
like a simple valid/ready stream on both directions
so even/odd parity has to be optional and switchable at runtime.
Firmware should be able to set the baud rate at runtime through a

options: AXI-Stream-style valid/ready for TX in and RX out
Register/strobe interface
decisions.choice: A valid/ready handshake on both directions. The TX sink accepts a byte when valid && ready. The RX source holds data and flags stable while valid && !ready.

options: Two runtime inputs parity_en and parity_odd shared by TX and RX
Separate TX/RX parity configs
Compile-time parameter
decisions.choice: Two runtime inputs, parity_en and parity_odd, shared by TX and RX. Each FSM latches them at the start of a frame.
decisions.rationale: The spec requires optional even/odd parity switchable at runtime. One link partner implies a shared setting. Latching at frame start avoids mid-frame corruption.
decisions.question: Should TX and RX share one parity setting, or do you need independent parity configuration per direction?

done_when: Port table is complete, with direction, width, clock domain, and reset value for every output.
The RX stream payload is defined as 8 data bits plus frame_err and parity_err sideband bits, aligned with that byte's valid.
The handshake rules (no combinational valid-on-ready dependency, data stable while stalled) are written down.

steps.title: Parameterize the core so the clock frequency is never hard-coded
steps.goal: Define the Parameters section: divider width, FIFO depth, and sync stages. Show that a runtime divider covers 9600 and 115200 baud at both 50 MHz and 100 MHz with acceptable error.

don't hard-code it.

options: Runtime divider only; no clock-frequency parameter in RTL
CLK_FREQ parameter plus runtime baud select
Both CLK_FREQ (for a reset-default divider) and runtime divider
decisions.choice: A runtime divider input with a parameterized width. The RTL contains no clock-frequency constant.
decisions.rationale: The spec asks not to hard-code the clock and to set baud via a divider at runtime.

options: Parameter FIFO_DEPTH default 8 (power of 2)
Fixed 8
Larger default (16)
decisions.choice: A FIFO_DEPTH parameter, default 8, used for both TX and RX FIFOs.
decisions.rationale: The spec suggests 8 bytes. Parameterizing costs nothing.

done_when: Parameter table lists DIV_WIDTH, FIFO_DEPTH, and SYNC_STAGES with default values and legal ranges.
A worked table gives the divider value and resulting baud error for 9600 and 115200 at 50 MHz and 100 MHz, with all errors under 2%.
DIV_WIDTH is shown to be wide enough for 9600 baud at 100 MHz.

steps.title: Design the 16x oversample tick generator driven by the runtime divider
steps.goal: Specify the baud tick counter that produces a single-cycle enable at 16x the baud rate, shared by RX sampling and TX bit timing. Define the divider semantics and what happens when the divider changes or is zero.

spec_evidence.quote: The receiver should oversample at 16x and sample in the middle of each bit.

decisions.topic: Divider semantics and baud generator structure
options: Integer divider = clk/(16*baud) producing one shared 16x tick for RX and TX
Divider = clk/baud with separate per-bit counters
Fractional (accumulator) divider
decisions.choice: An integer divider giving clk cycles per 16x tick (div = round(f_clk/(16*baud))). One free-running tick generator is shared by RX and TX, and TX advances one bit every 16 ticks.
decisions.rationale: Integer error is about 0.5% at 115200 for both 50 and 100 MHz, which is well within UART tolerance. This is the simplest and most common structure.
decisions.question: Should the firmware divider value be clock cycles per 16x oversample tick (clk/(16*baud)) or clock cycles per bit (clk/baud)?

done_when: Divider formula and counter behaviour (reload, tick pulse width of 1 clk) are specified.
Behaviour for divider = 0 or 1 is defined (clamp or hold idle).
Behaviour when the divider changes mid-frame is defined (takes effect at the next tick reload).

steps.title: Specify the RX front end: synchronizer, glitch filter, and false-start rejection
steps.goal: Define how the asynchronous rxd pin is synchronized, filtered against noise, and how a start bit is qualified. A short low glitch on an idle line must never launch a frame.

spec_evidence.quote: noisy, so some glitch filtering would be appreciated.
Please also make sure a short glitch
on the idle line isn't taken as a start bit.

options: Majority vote of 3 oversamples around mid-bit (ticks 7,8,9)
Continuous N-sample debounce filter ahead of the FSM
Both
decisions.choice: A 2-FF synchronizer, followed by a 3-sample majority vote at oversample ticks 7/8/9 of every bit, including the start bit.
decisions.rationale: This is standard practice (16550-style), rejects glitches shorter than about 1/16 bit without adding latency, and keeps the mid-bit sampling the spec requested.
decisions.question: Is a 3-of-3 majority vote at mid-bit sufficient glitch filtering, or do you need a stronger continuous debounce filter on the RX line?

options: Detect falling edge, then re-verify low at mid-start-bit (majority); abort to IDLE if high
Accept on falling edge
decisions.choice: A falling edge arms the receiver. If the majority-voted mid-start sample is high, the receiver aborts to IDLE without producing a byte.
decisions.rationale: The spec explicitly forbids treating a short idle-line glitch as a start bit.

done_when: Synchronizer depth and metastability argument are documented.
The maximum glitch width rejected is stated in oversample ticks.
The abort path from START_CHECK back to IDLE is shown in the FSM diagram.

steps.title: Define the RX frame FSM with per-byte frame/parity error tagging
steps.goal: Specify the RX FSM states (IDLE, START, DATA x8 LSB first, PARITY optional, STOP), the shift register, the parity check, and the stop-bit check. Errors must be tied to the exact byte they affect.

spec_evidence.quote: Frame format is the usual 8 data bits, 1 stop bit, LSB first.
bad stop bit or a parity mismatch, the CPU needs to know which byte was affected, not just
that an error happened at some point.

options: Store frame_err/parity_err with each byte in the RX FIFO (10-bit entries) and output them as RX stream sideband
Drop erroneous bytes and count errors
Separate error FIFO
decisions.choice: Errored bytes are still pushed. Each RX FIFO entry is {parity_err, frame_err, data[7:0]}, and the flags appear as sideband on the RX stream with that byte.
decisions.rationale: This is the only option that tells the CPU which byte was bad while keeping order. It costs 2 extra bits per FIFO entry.
decisions.question: Should bytes with framing or parity errors still be delivered to the CPU, tagged with error flags alongside the data, or discarded?

decisions.topic: Receiver behaviour after a framing error / break
options: Wait for line to return high (idle) before re-arming start detection
Re-arm immediately after stop sample
Additionally report a break flag
decisions.choice: After a bad stop bit, the receiver waits for rxd to be high before re-arming. No separate break flag is generated; a break shows up as a byte of 0x00 with frame_err.
decisions.rationale: This prevents a held-low line from flooding the FIFO with error bytes. Break reporting was not requested.
decisions.question: Do you need explicit break-condition detection, or is reporting a long low line as a single 0x00 byte with a framing error acceptable?

done_when: The FSM state diagram has transitions gated by the 16x tick and a bit counter.
Parity is computed as XOR of the data bits, with the odd/even selection defined, and the parity state is skipped when disabled.
The stop bit is sampled at mid-bit, and the byte plus flags are pushed when that sample is taken (no need to wait for the full stop bit).

steps.title: Define the TX path: FIFO-fed shift register with optional parity and stop bit
steps.goal: Specify the TX FSM, which pops the TX FIFO, sends start, 8 data bits LSB first, optional parity, and stop. Bit timing is every 16 ticks, and back-to-back frames run with no gaps. txd idles high.

spec_evidence.quote: Frame format is the usual 8 data bits, 1 stop bit, LSB first. Some GPS modules use parity,
like a simple valid/ready stream on both directions

done_when: The TX FSM and shift register are specified, with txd registered (glitch-free output).
Parity config is latched at the TX frame start.
Back-to-back throughput is defined: the next start bit begins immediately after the stop bit when the FIFO is non-empty.

steps.title: Specify TX and RX synchronous FIFOs and the RX overflow policy
steps.goal: Define both FIFOs (width, depth, full/empty logic, pointer scheme). Settle exactly what happens and what is signalled when a byte arrives and the RX FIFO is full.

spec_evidence.quote: The CPU is slow to service interrupts, so put a small FIFO on each side (8 bytes is
If the RX FIFO overflows we must know about it.

options: Drop incoming byte; assert sticky overflow flag cleared by an input pulse
Drop incoming byte; emit single-cycle overflow pulse (wrapper makes it sticky)
Overwrite oldest; tag next delivered byte with overrun flag
decisions.choice: The incoming byte is dropped and FIFO contents are preserved. A sticky rx_overflow output is set, cleared by an rx_overflow_clr input, and a one-cycle pulse is also provided for the wrapper's interrupt logic.
decisions.rationale: Preserving already-received data is the 16550 convention. The sticky flag guarantees a slow CPU sees it, and the pulse lets the wrapper count events or raise an interrupt.
decisions.question: When the RX FIFO is full and a new byte arrives, should the new byte be dropped (keeping older data), and should overflow be a sticky flag cleared by the wrapper or a one-cycle pulse?

done_when: FIFO widths are stated: TX 8 bits, RX 10 bits (data + 2 error flags).
Full/empty/count outputs available to the wrapper are listed.
Simultaneous push and pop when full or empty is defined.
The overflow flag set/clear timing is defined, including a clear coinciding with a new overflow.

steps.title: Assemble the block diagram and end-to-end timing/latency
steps.goal: Draw the top-level block diagram (tick gen, RX sync/filter, RX FSM, RX FIFO, TX FIFO, TX FSM) and document latencies. These are the stream-accept to start-bit delay and the stop-bit sample to rx_valid delay, plus sustained throughput at maximum baud.

done_when: The block diagram shows every module and every signal crossing between modules.
Latency numbers are given in clock cycles and oversample ticks for both directions.
A timing waveform is included for one 8N1 frame and one 8E1 frame with mid-bit sample points marked.

steps.title: Define clocking, reset, and the asynchronous rxd crossing
steps.goal: State that the design has one clock domain with rxd as the only asynchronous input. Define the reset style and reset values: txd high, FIFOs empty, FSMs idle, overflow cleared.

spec_evidence.quote: Our system clock is 50 MHz, but other projects run at 100 MHz, so please
The line is

options: Asynchronous assert, synchronous deassert, active-low
Fully synchronous active-high
decisions.choice: Active-low reset, asserted asynchronously and deasserted synchronously (synchronizer is the integrator's responsibility). txd resets high.
decisions.rationale: This is a common FPGA/ASIC-portable choice. It matters little architecturally, but must match the wrapper team's convention.
decisions.question: What reset convention should the UART use to match the wrapper and board: active-low async or active-high synchronous?

done_when: The single clock domain is documented, and rxd is identified as the only CDC point, with its synchronizer.
Reset values are listed for every state element that is visible at outputs.
txd is guaranteed to idle high during and after reset.

steps.title: Enumerate corner cases: runtime reconfiguration, noise, errors, and FIFO extremes
steps.goal: Collect all edge behaviours in one place. These are divider or parity changes mid-frame, divider 0, a glitch on idle, a glitch mid-bit, a break, back-to-back RX frames with minimal stop, RX overflow while the CPU stalls, a TX stream stall, and a reset mid-frame.

done_when: Each corner case has a defined expected behaviour referencing the relevant FSM state.
The baud mismatch tolerance of the RX sampling scheme is computed and stated.
Simultaneous frame and parity errors on one byte are defined (both flags set).

Record the remaining assumptions and open questions.

A scoreboard checks per-byte error-flag alignment with data.
